title: YOU ARE EXHAUSTED BECAUSE YOU KEEP RUNNING A RACE GOD NEVER ASKED YOU TO RUN
paragraphs: YOU ARE EXHAUSTED BECAUSE YOU KEEP RUNNING A RACE GOD NEVER ASKED YOU TO RUN
“Run With Endurance the Race Set Before Us” — The Heartbreaking Cost of Comparing Your Journey to Someone Else’s, and the Freedom of Finally Fixing Your Eyes on Jesus.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot cure.

You wake up tired. You pray, but your thoughts keep wandering. You open your Bible, but somewhere between the verses, you find yourself wondering why everyone else seems to be moving forward while you are still struggling with the same things you begged God to change years ago.
Someone your age is already married.
Someone you grew up with is financially secure.
Someone who started serving God long after you did now seems to have a flourishing ministry.
Someone who once asked you for advice is living the life you thought you would have by now.
And you?
You are still praying.
Still waiting.

Still trying to make sense of the doors that closed, the people who left, the prayers that seem unanswered, and the dreams that no longer look the way they did when you first surrendered your life to Jesus.
You smile when they announce their blessings.
You congratulate them.
You even whisper, “Praise God.”
But sometimes, when nobody is watching, another question slips out of your wounded heart.
“Lord, what about me?”
And perhaps the most painful part is not that you are struggling.
It is that you have started interpreting someone else's progress as evidence that God has forgotten you.
But what if the race exhausting you is not the race God actually set before you?

What if you have spent years measuring your obedience against someone else's opportunities, your healing against someone else's testimony, and your hidden faithfulness against someone else's visible success?
What if you have been running so desperately to catch up with people that you have slowly stopped looking at the One who called you to follow Him?
There is something Jesus wants you to understand before comparison steals another season of your life.
And it begins with a passage that many Christians have heard, but fewer have allowed to confront the way they live.
Hebrews 12:1–2 says:
“Let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith.” (KJV, excerpts)
Read those words again.
Not the race set before your neighbor.
Not the race set before the person whose testimony receives thousands of reactions.
Not the race set before the Christian whose life appears perfectly arranged.
The race set before US.
The original Greek makes this even more powerful.
The phrase is:
δι’ ὑπομονῆς τρέχωμεν τὸν προκείμενον ἡμῖν ἀγῶνα
di’ hypomonēs trechōmen ton prokeimenon hēmin agōna
A careful translation is:
“Let us run with endurance the contest set before us.”
The word ὑπομονή (hypomonē) means endurance, perseverance, or steadfastness under difficulty.
It does not describe a person who never gets tired.
It describes the kind of steadfastness that continues through hardship.
The word ἀγών (agōn) refers to a contest, struggle, or demanding competition. It is the word behind our English word agony.
And προκείμενον (prokeimenon) carries the sense of something lying before or being set before someone.
Notice something important.
Hebrews does not promise an effortless race.
It calls believers to endurance precisely because following Christ involves real struggle.
And while the passage speaks collectively to the Christian community rather than explicitly declaring that every believer has an entirely separate race, its application is deeply personal.
We are called to persevere in the life of faith before us, not to make another person's circumstances the standard of our worth.
Your responsibilities may differ.
Your opportunities may differ.
Your burdens may differ.
Your season may differ.
But the direction of every faithful Christian life remains the same.
Toward Jesus.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are not simply tired from serving God.
We are tired from trying to prove that God is doing something important with our lives.
We want visible evidence.
We want progress that other people can recognize.
We want a testimony impressive enough to silence those who doubted us.
We want the people who abandoned us to see what they lost.
We want those who underestimated us to discover that we became somebody.
And without realizing it, we begin using spiritual language to cover an old wound.
We say we want to glorify God.
But sometimes, buried underneath that sincere desire, there is another longing.
We want to be seen.
We want to matter.
We want our suffering to finally produce something people will applaud.
And Jesus, who sees beyond the words we speak, loves us too much to leave that hunger unexamined.
Because there is a terrible danger in running for the applause of people while convincing yourself that you are running for the glory of God.
You can be busy in ministry and spiritually distracted.
You can be publicly celebrated and privately empty.
You can spend years building something impressive while neglecting the quiet obedience Christ has actually placed before you.
And you can appear to be winning while losing sight of the Savior.
Do you remember Peter?
After the resurrection, Jesus met His disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias.
Peter had already experienced one of the most devastating failures of his life.
He had promised unwavering loyalty to Jesus.
He had declared that even if everyone else fell away, he would not.
But when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing the Lord.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine hearing your own voice saying, “I know not the man” (Matthew 26:74, KJV), while remembering the eyes of the Savior you had sworn never to abandon.
Peter had failed publicly.
Not because he lacked religious vocabulary.
Not because he had never witnessed a miracle.
Not because he had never loved Jesus.
He had failed because, in a moment of fear, his courage collapsed.
Yet the risen Christ did not discard him.
In John 21, Jesus questioned Peter three times about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
This was not a denial of Peter's failure.
It was restoration in the presence of the One he had denied.
And then Jesus told Peter something sobering.
His future would involve suffering, and his death would glorify God.
Then came the command.
“Follow me.” (John 21:19, KJV)
Two words.
Simple enough for a child to understand.
Costly enough to demand an entire life.
Not your reputation.
Not your former failure.
Not your need to prove yourself.
Me.
But what happened next reveals something astonishing about the human heart.
Peter turned around and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved.
And suddenly, instead of focusing on what Jesus had just told him, Peter asked:
“Lord, and what shall this man do?” (John 21:21, KJV)
There it is.
The question that has quietly haunted countless believers.
What about him?
What about her?
What about their future?
What about their calling?
What about their blessings?
Jesus answered:
“If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.” (John 21:22, KJV)
In the Greek, the closing command is:
σύ μοι ἀκολούθει
sy moi akolouthei
“You, follow Me.”
The pronoun σύ (sy), meaning “you,” is explicit and emphatic.
Jesus was redirecting Peter's attention away from speculation about another disciple's future and back to his own responsibility to follow Christ.
Jesus was not teaching that Christians should stop caring about one another.
He was confronting a distraction.
Peter did not need to understand John's future in order to obey Jesus in his own.
And perhaps that is the word your heart needs today.
You do not need to understand why God has allowed someone else's life to unfold differently before you can faithfully follow Jesus in yours.
You do not need their marriage.
Their platform.
Their income.
Their recognition.
Their opportunities.
Their timeline.
You need Christ.
And you need the grace to obey Him where you are.
Because comparison does something cruel.
It makes you despise blessings that would once have brought you to tears.
There was a time when you prayed for the things you now barely notice.
You prayed for another chance.
You prayed for peace.
You prayed for a door to open.
You prayed for strength to survive a season you thought would destroy you.
And God sustained you through days you were not sure you could endure.
Yet somewhere along the way, you began looking at someone else's life so intensely that you stopped recognizing the mercies present in your own.
Not every mercy arrives as a promotion.
Not every answered prayer becomes a public testimony.
Sometimes God's kindness is found in the strength to confess a sin you once defended.
Sometimes it is the courage to apologize.
Sometimes it is the grace to forgive someone who never asked for forgiveness.
Sometimes it is the ability to open your Bible again after months of spiritual numbness.
Sometimes it is simply this:
You are still turning toward Jesus.
And although perseverance does not earn salvation, it matters deeply because the God who saves His people also calls them to continue in faith.
Consider the apostle Paul.
When he approached the end of his life, he did not announce that he had become more successful than the other apostles.
He did not compare the number of people who knew his name.
He did not measure his life by comfort, influence, or worldly achievement.
He wrote:
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.” (2 Timothy 4:7, KJV)
The Greek word translated “course” is δρόμος (dromos), meaning a course or race.
Paul's confidence was not that he had outrun everyone else.
He had remained faithful to the calling entrusted to him.
And even that faithfulness was not something he could boast about independently of God's grace.
Paul had already declared:
“By the grace of God I am what I am.” (1 Corinthians 15:10, KJV)
Think about who wrote those words.
A man who once persecuted the church.
A man who had approved of violence against believers.
A man whose past contained things he could never undo.
Yet Jesus Christ met him in his rebellion, brought him to repentance, and transformed him into a witness of the very Gospel he once opposed.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your past never happened.
Not God calling evil good.
Not God offering cheap reassurance while leaving your heart unchanged.
Grace is God saving sinners through Jesus Christ, forgiving them through His sacrifice, and transforming them by His Spirit.
The scandal of Paul's past did not have the final word.
Jesus did.
And that is why our message remains:
Perhaps your scandal was never public.
Perhaps nobody knows what happened behind the closed door.
Nobody knows the addiction you are fighting.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The secret jealousy.
The compromise.
The prayerlessness.
The resentment you feel whenever someone else receives the blessing you desperately wanted.
Perhaps the person everyone calls “strong in the Lord” is quietly struggling to believe that God still cares.
And you have become so skilled at encouraging others that nobody realizes how desperately you need encouragement yourself.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to perform spiritual strength to come to Jesus.
You do not have to pretend you are winning.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony that sounds impressive.
You can tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I am jealous.”
“Lord, I am afraid.”
“Lord, I have been comparing myself to everyone.”
“Lord, I have been more concerned with being admired than being obedient.”
“Lord, I have been running for the wrong reasons.”
That kind of honesty may feel uncomfortable.
But confession is not the enemy of grace.
It is the abandonment of hiding before the God who already knows us.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV)
And if this has exposed something you have been hiding, you can begin with a simple prayer:
“Jesus, forgive me. Teach me to follow You.”
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggle to make that prayer sincere.
Someone else reading those words may discover that they are not the only person struggling to keep their eyes on Christ.
Now return to Hebrews 12.
Because the passage does not merely tell us to run.
It tells us what must happen if we are going to endure.
“Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us.” (Hebrews 12:1, KJV)
Notice the distinction.
Every weight.
And the sin.
The passage calls believers to cast off what hinders their endurance and the sin that entangles them.
Not every burden is itself sinful.
But something can become spiritually unhelpful when it repeatedly pulls your attention away from faithful obedience.
Even something ordinary.
Even something widely accepted.
Even something everyone else seems to be doing.
Perhaps you open Facebook to check on a friend.
Twenty minutes later, you feel like a failure.
You have compared your home to someone else's house.
Your marriage to someone else's anniversary pictures.
Your ministry to someone else's attendance numbers.
Your appearance to someone else's edited photographs.
Your financial situation to someone else's vacation.
And by the time you put your phone down, gratitude has turned into discontentment.
Nothing about your actual circumstances changed during those twenty minutes.
But your interpretation of your life did.
And suddenly, the blessings in your hands seemed small because you had spent so long staring at the blessings in someone else's.
Maybe the weight you need to lay aside is not social media itself.
Maybe it is the habit of treating every glimpse of another person's success as a verdict against your own life.
Maybe it is the constant need for approval.
Maybe it is the fear of being forgotten.
Maybe it is the belief that if you are not moving quickly, God must not be working.
And maybe repentance begins when you stop asking Jesus to help you win a competition He never commanded you to enter.
Because the race of faith is not an invitation to self-obsession.
It is a call to Christ-centered endurance.
Hebrews 12:2 gives us the focus:
“Looking unto Jesus.”
In Greek:
ἀφορῶντες εἰς Ἰησοῦν
aphorōntes eis Iēsoun
The participle ἀφορῶντες (aphorōntes) expresses the action of looking attentively toward someone or something, with the sense of directing one's gaze away from distractions.
The passage identifies Jesus as the ἀρχηγός (archēgos) and τελειωτής (teleiōtēs) of faith.
These words are translated in the KJV as “author and finisher.”
They present Jesus as the pioneer or founder and perfecter of faith.
He is not merely standing at the finish line waiting to see whether you can impress Him.
He is the crucified and risen Savior on whom your faith depends.
The passage continues by telling us that Jesus endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy set before Him, and is seated at the right hand of God's throne.
Do you see the contrast?
We become distracted by the approval of people.
Jesus endured the shame of the cross.
We become discouraged when our path involves suffering.
Jesus endured suffering in obedience to the Father's saving purpose.
We want a crown without discomfort.
Jesus bore the cross before entering into the glory of His exaltation.
And because He died and rose again, our hope rests not in how impressive our performance appears, but in the Savior who accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
The Gospel does not say, “Run fast enough and God will finally love you.”
The Gospel announces that salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that same grace creates a new life of obedience (Ephesians 2:10).
We do not run to purchase God's forgiveness.
We run because Christ has called us to follow Him.
We do not endure to become our own saviors.
We endure while trusting the Savior who has already conquered sin and death.
That changes everything.
Because when your identity is rooted in Christ, another person's success no longer has to threaten you.
You can rejoice when someone else is blessed.
You can celebrate a ministry growing without despising your own quiet service.
You can attend a wedding without deciding that your singleness makes you less valuable.
You can congratulate someone on a promotion without assuming that God has abandoned your financial struggles.
You can admire another believer's gifts without treating your own gifts as worthless.
You can learn from others without needing to become them.
And when you stumble, you can repent and return to Christ rather than surrendering to despair.
Because your value is not determined by how quickly you reach a milestone.
Your life is not meaningless because it looks different from someone else's.
And God's faithfulness is not measured by whether He gives every believer the same earthly circumstances.
Some Christians will experience visible fruit.
Others will serve faithfully in places the world barely notices.
Some will enjoy material abundance.
Others will endure poverty, persecution, illness, or profound loss.
Scripture does not promise identical outcomes.
But it does call every believer to the same Lord.
And it gives us a Savior who knows suffering.
There is another detail in Hebrews 12 that we cannot afford to miss.
The race is set before us.
This is not a call to isolated Christianity.
The chapter follows Hebrews 11, where the writer recounts men and women who lived by faith, often through extraordinary hardship.
Hebrews 12:1 refers to a “great cloud of witnesses.”
These are the faithful people whose lives testify to the reality of trusting God, not a promise that departed believers are watching our every move like spectators in a stadium.
Their testimonies remind us that faithfulness has always involved endurance.
And the wider letter of Hebrews repeatedly urges believers to encourage one another and not abandon gathering together.
That means your race is personal, but it is not meant to be lonely.
You need the Word.
You need prayer.
You need the fellowship of believers.
You need brothers and sisters who will remind you of the Gospel when your emotions are loud and your faith feels weak.
You need people who will celebrate your repentance more than your reputation.
People who will tell you the truth in love.
People who will point you back to Jesus when comparison has pulled your eyes away from Him.
And perhaps someone you know needs that encouragement today.
A friend who feels left behind.
A parent exhausted from carrying responsibilities nobody sees.
A young believer who thinks their life is already ruined.
A church worker who keeps showing up but feels spiritually empty.
A family member who believes their past disqualifies them from grace.
Or send it privately with a simple message:
“I thought of you. Keep your eyes on Jesus.”
Because it probably will.
There will be another announcement.
Another promotion.
Another engagement.
Another testimony.
Another moment when the old question tries to rise again.
“Lord, what about me?”
When it does, return to the words Jesus spoke to Peter.
“Follow thou me.”
Not because your pain is imaginary.
Not because waiting is easy.
Not because every disappointment will make sense in this lifetime.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust even when you cannot see the entire road ahead.
And there is a beautiful way we can help one another remain grounded in that truth.
At Gospel Warrior, our desire is not simply to publish messages that stir emotions for a moment.
We want people to open their Bibles, understand Scripture faithfully, turn away from sin, grow in prayer, and follow Jesus when the excitement of an inspiring message has faded.
We want wounded believers to encounter the truth of God's grace.
We want those drifting from faith to hear the call to repentance.
We want seekers to understand that the heart of Christianity is not self-improvement, but the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And we want those who have already experienced God's mercy to become stronger, wiser, more discerning disciples.
These resources are intended to help believers go deeper into Scripture, strengthen their understanding of biblical truth, and nourish their daily walk with Jesus.
It is not.
But because voluntary, generous support can become a meaningful expression of Christian stewardship when it is given freely, prayerfully, and for the glory of God.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
The principle still challenges us to give without coercion, manipulation, or resentment.
Think of it as a voluntary ministry offering, given from a willing heart, rather than a replacement for the biblical responsibilities of generosity and church stewardship.
Those items are simply a token of appreciation.
The greater purpose is the Gospel.
A resource placed in someone's hands.
A Scripture understood more clearly.
A believer encouraged to keep going.
A struggling soul reminded that forgiveness is found in Christ.
A family drawn into a meaningful conversation about Jesus.
We cannot promise that every article will reach a particular person or produce a particular outcome.
But we can faithfully sow the Word, serve with integrity, and trust God with the fruit.
You are no less welcome.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The free resources remain an invitation to learn and grow.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
It is possible to become so focused on what we are building that we forget whom we are following.
We never want Gospel Warrior to become the finish line.
Jesus is the One we want people to see.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the person who started reading this article with a tired heart.
The person who has spent months wondering why life seems to be moving so slowly.
The person who secretly feels ashamed of not being further along.
The person who has watched others celebrate milestones while quietly carrying grief.
The person who wonders whether years of ordinary faithfulness have meant anything.
I wish I could tell you exactly when the waiting will end.
I cannot.
I wish I could promise that every dream you surrendered will eventually return in a better form.
Scripture gives us no such universal promise.
I wish I could tell you that obedience will always lead to comfort, recognition, financial security, and earthly success.
But that would not be the Gospel Jesus preached.
What I can tell you is this.
Jesus Christ is worthy of following even when the road is painful.
His resurrection means death does not have the final word.
His sacrifice means repentant sinners can receive forgiveness.
His grace means your worst failure does not have to become the final definition of your life.
And His call to follow Him remains meaningful whether your obedience is noticed by thousands or witnessed by no one but God.
Maybe today you need to stop chasing the life you thought would prove your worth.
Maybe you need to confess that envy has been poisoning your gratitude.
Maybe you need to surrender a dream that has become more important to you than Christ.
Maybe you need to stop using someone else's blessings as evidence against God's goodness.
Maybe you need to return to the simple obedience you have been avoiding while waiting for a dramatic sign.
Pray.
Open the Scriptures.
Confess what needs confessing.
Make the apology.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek help where you need help.
Serve faithfully with the gifts you have been given.
Encourage someone else without making their blessing about your disappointment.
And when you fall, do not make peace with sin.
Return to the Savior.
Because the call to endurance is not the call to pretend you are invincible.
It is the call to keep trusting Jesus.
One day, the race of earthly life will end.
The applause of people will fade.
The numbers on our screens will become irrelevant.
The comparisons that consumed so many of our thoughts will lose their power.
And what will matter is not whether we lived someone else's story.
It will be whether our hope was truly in Jesus Christ.
Whether we belonged to Him.
Whether His grace was transforming us.
Whether we persevered in the faith.
Whether, by His mercy, we could say with Paul:
“I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”
If this message has reached a place in your heart that you have struggled to explain, I would love to hear from you.
You do not need to tell the whole world your private story.
But your honest words may remind another weary believer that they are not alone.
But above everything else, keep your eyes on Jesus.
Not on the person ahead of you.
Not on the person behind you.
Not on the applause.
Not on the shame.
Not on the life you thought you would have by now.
On Jesus.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who restores the fallen.
The One who calls His people to follow Him faithfully until the end.
You may have spent years grieving because you were not living someone else's story, while Jesus was calling you to be faithful in the one unfolding right beneath your feet.
